pos: n. (the projecting part of the body at the joint of the thigh)
etymology: From Old English hype, the hip or haunch, a common Germanic word. In the phrase hip and thigh it became a proverb for utter, unsparing overthrow.
biblical_def: After the Philistines burned his wife and her father with fire, Samson took vengeance on them: “And he smote them hip and thigh with a great slaughter: and he went down and dwelt in the top of the rock Etam.” The phrase pictures a fighter overthrowing his enemies so completely that limb is heaped upon limb, and it passed from this verse into English as a byword for total defeat. Samson's story is a strange mixture: a Nazarite from the womb, raised up to begin to deliver Israel (Judges 13:5), yet driven again and again by his own appetites and grievances. Here his personal revenge is nonetheless the instrument by which God strikes the Philistine oppressors, for the LORD “sought an occasion against the Philistines” (Judges 14:4). The Spirit of the LORD came upon him in power; his life was not thereby made a pattern of holiness. Hebrews numbers him among those who through faith “out of weakness were made strong” (Hebrews 11:32-34), a reminder that God's deliverances are His own work, done through flawed instruments, and point forward to the one Deliverer whose victory over His enemies is complete and whose life is without sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): HIP, the projecting part of an animal formed by the os ilium or haunch bone; the haunch. To have on the hip, to have the advantage over one.
webster_full: HIP, n. The projecting part of an animal formed by the os ilium or haunch bone; the haunch, or the flesh that covers the bone and the adjacent parts.
To smite hip and thigh, to overthrow completely; a phrase from Judges 15:8.
To have on the hip, to have the advantage over one.

He then dwelt in the top of the rock Etam.

Jdg 14:4
But his father and his mother knew not that it was of the LORD, that he sought an occasion against the Philistines: for at that time the Philistines had dominion over Israel.
And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:
corruption_summary: Samson is either sentimentalized as a simple hero or dismissed as a mere brute; both readings miss God's sovereign use of a flawed deliverer.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase hip and thigh survives as an idiom for complete overthrow.

The danger lies in how Samson is read. Children's-book heroism forgets his lusts and his ruin; cynical readings forget that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him and that Hebrews counts him among the faithful. Scripture holds both: God sovereignly uses weak and sinful men, and their sins still bring their own bitter harvest.

pos: n. (the projecting nose and mouth of a beast, especially of swine)
etymology: From Middle English snoute, related to Middle Dutch snute and Low German snut, the muzzle of an animal.
biblical_def: Solomon gives one of the most vivid pictures in Proverbs: “As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.” The jewel is real gold and truly beautiful, but set in the snout of an unclean animal that roots in the mire, it is wasted and mocked by its setting. So is outward beauty joined to a foolish, undiscerning heart. The proverb does not despise beauty, for Scripture praises the beauty of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Esther. It weighs beauty against discretion and finds that beauty without wisdom is degraded by the life that wears it. The same book ends with the verdict: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). Peter teaches the same, directing believing women to the adorning of “a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1 Peter 3:4). The proverb speaks to men as well: whatever gifts a person has, they are only as honourable as the wisdom that governs them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SNOUT, the long projecting nose of a beast, as of swine; the nose of a man, in contempt; the nozzle or end of a hollow pipe.
webster_full: SNOUT, n. The long projecting nose of a beast, as of swine.
The nose of a man; in contempt.
The nozzle or end of a hollow pipe.
Proverbs 11:22 compares a fair woman without discretion to a jewel of gold in a swine's snout.

scriptures: As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Modern culture exalts outward beauty as a woman's chief worth while mocking discretion, modesty and the fear of the LORD as repression, which is exactly the gold-in-the-snout exchange the proverb condemns.
corruption_paragraphs: An image-driven culture measures worth by appearance and treats discretion, modesty and restraint as obstacles to self-expression. Beauty is displayed, sold and worshipped, while the inward adorning Scripture prizes is dismissed as old-fashioned.

The proverb reverses that valuation. Beauty is a real good, but it is a jewel that needs a fit setting, and that setting is a discreet heart that fears God. Christian parents and churches should teach daughters and sons alike that the hidden man of the heart is of great price in God's sight.

pos: adj. (marked with small spots of colour on the skin)
etymology: From freckle, Middle English frekel, from Old Norse freknur, freckles. The Hebrew word in Leviticus names a harmless whitish eruption, a tetter.
biblical_def: Among the laws of leprosy in Leviticus 13, the priest was given careful tests to distinguish true uncleanness from harmless blemishes. One such case reads: “Then the priest shall look: and, behold, if the bright spots in the skin of their flesh be darkish white; it is a freckled spot that groweth in the skin; he is clean.” Not every mark on the skin was leprosy, and the priest was not to pronounce a man unclean on suspicion. The law shows God's care both for the purity of His camp and for justice to the individual: the leper was to be put outside, but the man with a freckled spot was not to be cast out wrongly. The priest's discerning eye anticipates the greater discernment of Christ, the great High Priest, who touched the leper and made him clean (Matthew 8:3). Leprosy in Scripture serves as a living picture of sin, which spreads, defiles and separates from God; but the law's care in distinguishing the freckled spot reminds the church to judge with righteous judgment, neither calling clean things unclean nor overlooking the true plague.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FRECKLED, spotted; having small yellowish spots on the skin or surface.
webster_full: FRECKLE, n. A spot of a yellowish color in the skin; any small spot or discoloration.
FRECKLED, a. Spotted; having small yellowish spots on the skin or surface.
Leviticus 13:39 calls a darkish white spot in the skin a freckled spot, and the man clean.

Mat 8:3

corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is righteous, careful judgment that neither condemns on suspicion nor ignores real defilement.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word keeps its plain sense.

The law of the freckled spot teaches discernment. Churches can err in both directions: condemning on rumour and appearance, or refusing to name genuine sin for fear of seeming judgmental. The priest was to look carefully and pronounce truly, and the Lord commands His people to judge not according to the appearance, but to judge righteous judgment (John 7:24).

etymology: From Latin putrefacere, to make rotten, from puter, rotten, and facere, to make. The Authorized Version spells it putrifying; the Hebrew speaks of a fresh, raw wound.
biblical_def: Isaiah opens his prophecy by describing the nation of Judah as a body beaten from head to foot: “From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment.” The people had been chastened again and again, yet they revolted more and more (Isaiah 1:5). Their sores festered because they were never brought to the Physician. The image is a diagnosis of sin: it is not a surface blemish but a corruption that runs through the whole body, head and heart included, and it does not heal itself. Yet Isaiah does not end with the diagnosis. In the same chapter the LORD calls, “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). Later the prophet shows the remedy: the Servant who “was wounded for our transgressions” and by whose stripes we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The festering wounds of sinners are bound up only by the wounds of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PUTREFY, to cause to rot or decay with an offensive smell; to corrupt; to become putrid. PUTREFYING, rotting; corrupting.
webster_full: PUTREFY, v.t. To cause to rot with an offensive smell; to corrupt.
PUTREFY, v.i. To rot; to dissolve, as organic matter.
PUTREFYING, ppr. Rotting; corrupting; becoming putrid.

The sores were neither closed, bound up nor mollified with ointment.
scriptures: Isa 1:6

Isa 1:5

Isa 53:5

corruption_summary: Sin is reframed as a wound done to us rather than a corruption within us, so that the festering sores of Isaiah 1:6 are treated with self-esteem and affirmation instead of repentance and the blood of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern moral vocabulary treats human brokenness as injury inflicted from outside. People are seen as victims of circumstances, systems or others, and the cure offered is affirmation and self-acceptance. That turns Isaiah's diagnosis upside down, for his putrifying sores belong to a rebellious people who would not turn.

Scripture names the disease as sin and the corruption as inward, from the sole of the foot to the head. No ointment of self-regard can close it. The only remedy is the wounded Servant of Isaiah 53, and the only way to Him is confession and repentance.

pos: v. (past tense; stopped from flowing, as blood)
etymology: From Old French estanchier, to stop or stay the flow, probably from a Latin root meaning to make weary or still. Related to staunch, firm.
biblical_def: A woman who had suffered an issue of blood twelve years, who had spent all her living on physicians and could not be healed of any, pressed through the crowd toward Jesus. She “Came behind him, and touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched.” Under the law her condition made her unclean and made unclean whatever she touched (Leviticus 15:25-27). But when she touched Christ, His holiness was not defiled; her uncleanness was cleansed. The healing was immediate and complete, and the Lord would not let her slip away unseen. He called her forward, and she confessed before all the people why she had touched Him. Then He said, “Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace” (Luke 8:48). Her faith was not a magic in the garment; it was trust in the Person who wore it. The stanched blood is a sign of the deeper cleansing Christ gives: what twelve years and all the physicians could not do, a touch of faith in Him accomplished in an instant, and He received her publicly as a daughter.

webster_full: STANCH, v.t. To stop or stay a flowing of blood; as, to stanch blood; to stanch a wound.
STANCH, v.i. To stop, as blood; to cease flowing.

Luk 8:43

Luk 8:48

corruption_summary: The miracle is misused either as a pattern for relic-power and prayer cloths or, by sceptical readings, as a psychosomatic recovery; both obscure the Person in whom she trusted.
corruption_paragraphs: Some have built on this account a theology of holy objects, selling anointed cloths and promising healing through contact. Others reduce the miracle to the power of belief over a nervous condition. Both miss the point Luke makes plain: the power went out of Christ Himself (Luke 8:46), and her faith was trust in Him.

The church honours the miracle by honouring its Lord. He is the One who cleanses the unclean without being defiled, who hears the trembling confession and calls the outcast daughter. Faith rests in Him, not in garments, rituals or the strength of our own believing.

pos: v. (past tense; expelled air suddenly and audibly through the nose)
etymology: From Middle English snesen, a variant of fnesen, from Old English fneosan, to sneeze, an imitative word.
biblical_def: The son of the Shunammite woman, the child promised to her through Elisha, had died in his mother's lap. Elisha came, shut the door, prayed to the LORD, and stretched himself upon the child. Then “he returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.” The sneeze is the first sign of breath returning to a body that had none, the most ordinary of bodily acts made extraordinary by the setting. Seven times, the number of completeness, the child sneezed, and life was fully restored. The miracle is one of the few resurrections in the Old Testament, and it was done in answer to prayer, for Elisha “prayed unto the LORD” (2 Kings 4:33). It foreshadows the greater power of Christ, who raised the widow's son at Nain and Jairus's daughter with a word, and who Himself rose from the dead as the firstfruits of them that slept. Hebrews remembers such mothers: “Women received their dead raised to life again” (Hebrews 11:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SNEEZE, to emit air through the nose audibly and violently, by a kind of involuntary convulsive force.
webster_full: SNEEZE, v.i. To emit air through the nose audibly and violently, by a kind of involuntary convulsive force occasioned by irritation of the inner membrane of the nose.
SNEEZE, n. A sudden and violent ejection of air through the nose with an audible sound.

scriptures: Then he returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
He went in therefore, and shut the door upon them twain, and prayed unto the LORD.

corruption_summary: Sceptical readings explain the raising as resuscitation from a coma, denying both the death and the miracle the text plainly records.
corruption_paragraphs: Naturalistic commentary has long tried to tame the Old Testament resurrections, suggesting the child was only unconscious and that Elisha performed something like artificial respiration. The text gives no room for it: the child sat on his mother's knees till noon, and then died (2 Kings 4:20), and the mother herself treated him as dead.

The account is a true miracle of the living God, answered to prayer through His prophet. It belongs with the raisings by Elijah and by Christ as testimony that God is Lord over death, and it anticipates the bodily resurrection of all His people at the last day.

etymology: From un-, reversing, and clothed, from Old English clathian, to clothe. Paul's Greek ekduo means to put off a garment.
biblical_def: Paul compares the present body to a tent, an earthly house of this tabernacle, which will be dissolved. He then writes: “For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.” The believer does not long simply to escape the body, to be a naked soul. Death, which separates soul from body, is an unclothing, and though to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), that state is not the final hope. The groaning of the Christian is for the resurrection body, the house from heaven, when what is mortal will be swallowed up of life. This is the Reformed and biblical doctrine of the intermediate state and the resurrection held together: the souls of the righteous are made perfect in holiness and received into the highest heavens, awaiting the full redemption of their bodies (1689 Confession, 31.1). Christianity is not escape from matter; it is the redemption of the whole man, body and soul, and the earnest of it is the Spirit (2 Corinthians 5:5).

webster_full: UNCLOTHE, v.t. To strip of clothes; to make naked; to divest.
UNCLOTHED, pp. Stripped of clothing; divested.
2 Corinthians 5:4 says believers groan, not to be unclothed but clothed upon.
Mortality is to be swallowed up of life in the resurrection.

scriptures: For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
corruption_summary: Popular piety reduces the Christian hope to the soul's escape from the body, a Gnostic-flavoured unclothing that forgets the resurrection of the body Paul longs for.
corruption_paragraphs: Much popular Christianity speaks as though the goal of salvation were to shed the body and float to heaven as a spirit. That is closer to Plato and the Gnostics than to Paul. The body is not a prison to be escaped; it is a tent to be replaced with a house from God, and the whole man will be raised.

Scripture holds the true order: at death the believer's soul goes immediately to be with Christ, which is far better; at the last day the body is raised incorruptible. Paul does not long to be unclothed, but clothed upon. Christian funerals, hope and ethics of the body should all be shaped by that resurrection hope.

etymology: From Middle English struglen, of uncertain origin, perhaps imitative or related to Scandinavian words meaning to strive. The Hebrew speaks of crushing or thrusting one another.
biblical_def: Rebekah, barren until Isaac entreated the LORD for her, conceived twins: “And the children struggled together within her; and she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to enquire of the LORD.” The answer explained the struggle: “Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). The struggle in the womb was the beginning of a conflict between Jacob and Esau, and between Israel and Edom, that runs through the whole Old Testament. Paul takes this very moment as a proof of sovereign election: before the children were born, “neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth” (Romans 9:11), it was said, the elder shall serve the younger. The struggle shows that God's choice was made before any merit or demerit could exist. Grace does not wait for the outcome of human striving; it determines it.

webster_full: STRUGGLE, v.i. To strive, or to make efforts with a twisting or with contortions of the body.
To use great efforts; to labor hard; to strive; to contend.

corruption_summary: Romans 9's use of the twins is evaded by reading election as merely national and corporate, or as God foreseeing who would believe, so that the struggle in the womb no longer proves anything about grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminian and corporate-election readings insist that Paul speaks only of nations, Israel and Edom, and not of individual salvation, or that God chose Jacob because He foresaw his faith. Paul shuts both doors: the choice was made before either child had done good or evil, not of works but of Him that calleth, and he goes on to answer the objection that this is unrighteous (Romans 9:14).

The 1689 Confession states the doctrine plainly: God has chosen some unto everlasting life, without any foresight of faith or good works as a condition moving Him (3.5). The twins' struggle stands at the head of that doctrine in Scripture, teaching that salvation is of the LORD from first to last.

pos: n. (a pile of sheaves of grain set up together in the field)
etymology: From Middle English schokke, related to Middle Dutch schok and Middle Low German schok, a heap of sheaves. Distinct from the shock that means a violent blow.
biblical_def: Eliphaz, though he misjudged Job's case, spoke a true word about the end of the righteous whom God chastens and delivers: “Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season.” A shock is a stack of sheaves set up in the field to ripen and dry before being carried to the barn. The picture is of a life ripened and gathered at the proper time, not cut down green but brought in full and ready, as a farmer brings in grain when it is fit. The margin gives the Hebrew sense of cometh in: “ascendeth,” as the sheaves are lifted up onto the cart. Death for the righteous is a harvest, not a destruction; the God of the harvest gathers His own in their season. Job's own end bore it out, for he “died, being old and full of days” (Job 42:17). The New Testament deepens the image, for Christ speaks of the harvest at the end of the world when the wheat is gathered into His barn (Matthew 13:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SHOCK, a pile or assemblage of sheaves of wheat, rye and the like, set up in a field, the sheaves being laid one against another.
webster_full: SHOCK, n. A pile or assemblage of sheaves of wheat, rye and the like, the sheaves being set up in a field, one against another.
SHOCK, v.t. To make up into shocks or piles of sheaves.
SHOCK (distinct word), a violent collision or concussion; an offense to the mind.
Job 5:26 compares the righteous man's death in full age to a shock of corn coming in in its season.
The margin renders cometh in as ascendeth.
scriptures: Job 5:26
Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season.

Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that the death of the righteous is a harvest in God's appointed season, not a meaningless end.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The agricultural sense has simply faded from common use.

The image is worth recovering in an age that hides death or treats it as pure loss. For those in Christ, death in its season is the gathering of ripe grain into the Lord's barn. Believers may grieve, but not as others which have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

pos: n. (a sudden burst of light, as of lightning)
etymology: From Middle English flasshen, to splash or dash, probably imitative. The sense of a sudden burst of light developed later.
biblical_def: In Ezekiel's vision by the river Chebar, the four living creatures that bore the throne-chariot of God moved with dazzling swiftness: “And the living creatures ran and returned as the appearance of a flash of lightning.” They went wherever the Spirit was to go, and they turned not when they went (Ezekiel 1:12). Their motion was like fire and lightning because they served the God whose glory filled the vision, the One seated on the throne above the firmament who had “the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD” (Ezekiel 1:28). The flash of lightning speaks of the speed and obedience of God's servants and of the overwhelming majesty of His presence. These creatures are the cherubim, as Ezekiel later recognized (Ezekiel 10:20). The same imagery reaches into the New Testament, where Christ says of His coming: “For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be” (Matthew 24:27). His return will be sudden, visible and unmistakable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FLASH, a sudden burst of light; a flood of light instantaneously appearing and disappearing; a sudden burst of something regarded as resembling light.
webster_full: FLASH, n. A sudden burst of light; a flood of light instantaneously appearing and disappearing; as a flash of lightning.
A sudden burst, as of wit or merriment.

corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is the majesty of God's throne and the swift obedience of those who serve Him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word keeps its ordinary sense.

Ezekiel's vision rebukes the casual familiarity with which modern worship often approaches God. The prophet fell on his face before the throne whose servants moved like lightning. Reverence and godly fear (Hebrews 12:28) are the fitting response to such a God, and swift, unswerving obedience is the pattern of His servants.
